title: Flow-Based Conformal Predictive Distributions
claim: Complex, high-dimensional structured outputs across scientific domains are hard to represent with prediction sets, which motivates making implicit sets usable.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, lettered (a)-(c), each a different domain's data
description: A single-row figure with three equal-width panels labeled (a), (b), (c), each with a title above it. Panel (a), 'Turbulent CFD Simulations', is a full-bleed teal-to-cream heatmap of swirling turbulent vortices. Panel (b), 'Precipitation Fields', is a map of North America with a rainbow-colored rainfall overlay (green, blue, yellow, red) concentrated over the central and eastern US and the Pacific Northwest. Panel (c), 'Tropical Cyclone Trajectories', is a map of the Atlantic basin covered by hundreds of overlapping multicolored track lines that fan out from the tropics to the northeast. The figure has no arrows, no method modules and no 'ours' highlighting. The eye goes first to the colorful precipitation map and the dense cyclone tracks. It shows examples of the complex output spaces where prediction sets are needed.
caption: What do prediction sets look like for CFD simulations? Precipitation patterns? Tropical Cyclones? How can we take implicitly defined sets and make them useful in these spaces?
abstract: Conformal prediction provides a distribution-free framework for uncertainty quantification via prediction sets with exact finite-sample coverage. In low dimensions these sets are easy to interpret, but in high-dimensional or structured output spaces they are difficult to represent and use, which can limit their ability to integrate with downstream tasks such as sampling and probabilistic forecasting. We show that any sufficiently regular differentiable nonconformity score induces a deterministic flow on the output space whose trajectories converge to the boundary of the corresponding conformal prediction set. This leads to a computationally efficient, training-free method for sampling conformal boundaries in arbitrary dimensions. Mixing across confidence levels yields conformal predictive distributions whose quantile regions coincide with the empirical conformal prediction sets. We provide an approximation bound decomposing CPD predictive error into score-induced distortion, base-measure quality, and gradient flow-induced distortion. We evaluate the approach on PDE inverse problems, precipitation downscaling, climate model debiasing, and hurricane trajectory forecasting.
